I don't want to take this issue too off topic, but is there also an explanation for why FED.US domains are included in this data set at all? Both the About and the [README](https://github.com/cisagov/dotgov-data/blob/main/README.md?plain=1#L4) suggest this repository is specifically for domains in the .gov zone. I guess the answer to that may dictate @pburkholder's request?
Thanks for flagging, @grandamp.

Fair questions – I'm going to take @hodgesmr diversion (cool bot BTW) before addressing @pburkholder's (back soon,  Peter).

CISA manages the registry for the .gov TLD _and also_ the `fed.us` public suffix. Our registry operator, Verisign, runs authoritative DNS for both:

```
$ dig +short ns fed.us
a.gov-servers.net.
c.gov-servers.net.
b.gov-servers.net.
d.gov-servers.net.

$ dig +short ns gov
d.gov-servers.net.
b.gov-servers.net.
a.gov-servers.net.
c.gov-servers.net.
```

That's why our data includes the fed.us "TLD" and the few registered "second-level domains" that exist – it's the same back- and front-end infrastructure. 

We anticipate retiring fed.us as a registerable namespace later this year, at which point there will be no more fed.us data here.

A couple thoughts:
* current-{full,federal} will only ever include .gov (...and some fed.us) data, so we won't add si.edu there. 
* Given https://www.si.edu/ogc/legalhistory, we have some questions as to whether Smithsonian is an "agency" under the DOTGOV Act, which we'll dig into more. (I'll note that SI registered `itis.gov` before the DOTGOV Act's passage.) So for now, it's at best premature for si.edu to be added to our non-.gov files.

More research on SI from @bengerman13:

[Smithsonian says](https://www.si.edu/ohr/faq) these things, which seem relevant:
> Is The Smithsonian Part of the Government?
> The Smithsonian is a Trust Instrumentality of the United States
> What are Trust Positions?
> [...] Trust employees are not part of the civil service, nor does trust fund employment lead to Federal status.

maybe this says otherwise? https://www.justice.gov/file/24096/download
> we conclude that the unique nature of the Smithsonian counsels in favor of determining the status of the Smithsonian on a statute-by-statute basis. In this instance, we adhere to our prior opinion that the Smithsonian is not covered by the FACA, and we conclude that the Smithsonian is an “executive agency” within the meaning of the Property Act

but also:
> The Smithsonian perceives itself as  “not a government agency in any ordinary use of the term, but [as] a charitable trust for the benefit of humankind whose trustee is the United States. As such, it cannot carry out the functions of any of the three branches of government, but must be devoted exclusively to its educational and scientific purposes ‘for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men."

Thanks for commenting again. 

We've chatted with SI and CISA folk, and it's clear that the right call for Smithsonian is to treat them on a statute-by-statute basis. Federal laws use the words "federal agency" to mean different (and sometimes conflicting) things. SI is not an "agency" under the definition of the DOTGOV Act ([6 USC 663(a)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:6%20section:665%20edition:prelim)%20OR%20(granuleid:USC-prelim-title6-section665)&f=treesort&edition=prelim&num=0&jumpTo=true)), but are a "Federal... government entity, or other publicly controlled entity". 

(Here's a useful [CRS report](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R44370.pdf) on SI.)

So, I believe si.edu would qualify as a US government domain, though not one to add to current-{full, federal}.csv.

Oh now this is confusing:

From [the website](https://oversightboard.pr.gov/about-us/):

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4592/201497297-f6c3c683-2ee7-4cbc-9e02-e0319a11cb35.png)

And [the founding act says](https://drive.google.com/file/d/13samB-s8eL7gbFwUVI46l8lrCl1WWj_e/view):

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4592/201497314-9d52b056-a225-4aff-9ba8-d5bd09600ebb.png)

So, I think this should be marked as a State domain and not a `Federal - Executive` domain - what do you think?

Same for `Corporation for National and Community Service, Office Of Inspector General`. Also, that field uses an `and` while the CNSC entries above it use an `&`, so opportunity for typographical consistency as well. ;)
Also, `cap.gov` and `capnho.gov` are marked as `Civil Air Patrol`, but that appears to be a component of the U.S. Air Force, which itself is a component of the Department of Defense.
Why does the promesa.gov domain exist? I checked historical DNS, it does not appear a website has ever been attached to that domain.

Interestingly, Armed Forces Retirement Home looks to be an `independent establishment in the executive branch`, according to its [founding statute](https://www.afrh.gov/sites/default/files/2021_24USC_Chapter10_AFRH_0.pdf), but according to its [org chart](https://www.afrh.gov/sites/default/files/20220310_AFRH_OrganizationChart.pdf), its CEO is a DoD employee and the COO is appointed by the secretary of DoD. I'm not recommending this be changed, since the statute seems clear, but documenting it here for the record.

Some others:

* `United States Postal Service, Office of Inspector General` (this appears twice, once for peacecorpsoig.gov, which looks like an error - will file separate issue)
* `United States International Trade Commission, Office of Inspector General`
* `Federal Housing Finance Agency, Office of Inspector General`

I realize that adds up to 5 examples - but there are at least as many counter-examples. So, it seems worth making it consistent, and I would recommend moving the OIG name to be designated in the `Office` since they are (though independent) a component of the parent agency.
